maths_eduqas_f.5.2.summary: Mastering the construction and interpretation of tables, charts, and diagrams is essential for the Eduqas Foundation tier. This revision guide covers categorical data (bar charts, pie charts, pictograms), discrete numerical data (frequency tables), and time series data (line graphs). You will learn how to extract values, calculate missing angles, spot trends over time, and accurately draw scales.

core.p: Categorical data places items into distinct groups or names. We organise raw data into frequency tables using tally marks to count occurrences efficiently.
bullets: Categories must be mutually exclusive and exhaustive.
Tally marks are grouped in blocks of five for easy counting.
The frequency column represents the total count for each category.

callouts.p: Data that can be sorted into non-overlapping groups or categories (e.g., eye colour, car brand).

core.p: Bar charts display categorical or discrete data using rectangular bars of equal width. The height or length of each bar represents the frequency.
bullets: Axes must be labelled clearly with units where applicable.
Equal gaps must be left between consecutive bars.
The scale must be linear, starting at zero and increasing by equal increments.

callouts.p: Do not let bars touch in a standard bar chart; touching bars are reserved for continuous grouped data (histograms).

core.p: Pictograms use symbols or pictures to represent quantities. A key is always provided to state what value a single symbol or half-symbol represents.
bullets: Always check the key first before calculating values.
Partial symbols represent fractional parts of the key value.
Align symbols neatly in rows for accurate comparison.

callouts.p: If a symbol represents 10 items, a half symbol represents 5 items and a quarter symbol represents 2.5 items.

core.p: Pie charts divide a circle into sectors proportional to the frequency of each category. The total frequency represents 360 degrees.
bullets: Calculate the angle per item using 360 divided by the total frequency.
Multiply each category frequency by the angle per item.
Check that all sector angles sum exactly to 360 degrees.

callouts.p: Sector angle = (Frequency / Total Frequency) x 360

core.p: Time series graphs display data collected over time, plotted with time on the horizontal axis and the variable on the vertical axis. Points are joined with straight line segments.
bullets: Time is always placed on the horizontal x-axis.
Points are connected with straight lines to highlight trends over time.
Do not extrapolate lines blindly beyond the given data points.

callouts.p: Look for overall upward trends, downward trends, or seasonal cyclical patterns.

core.p: Two-way tables display categorical data across two different variables simultaneously, using rows and columns with row and column totals.
bullets: Every row and column total must sum correctly.
Use subtraction to find missing inner cell values.
Check that the grand total matches both row totals and column totals.

callouts.p: Always verify that the sum of horizontal totals equals the sum of vertical totals in the bottom right cell.

core.p: Discrete numerical data represents exact countable values. Frequency tables list each distinct value alongside its frequency.
bullets: Values are arranged in ascending numerical order.
Frequencies represent how many times each specific value occurred.
Total frequency (N) is found by summing the frequency column.

callouts.p: Numerical data that can only take specific exact values, usually obtained by counting (e.g., shoe size, number of pets).

core.p: Composite or stacked bar charts display multivariate categorical data by stacking sub-categories on top of each other within a single bar.
bullets: Each section height represents the frequency of that sub-category.
A clear legend or key must explain the shading or colours used.
Total bar height represents the combined total for that main category.

callouts.p: To find the frequency of a middle section, subtract the lower boundary value from the upper boundary value.

core.p: Dual bar charts place two bars side-by-side for each category to compare two different sets of data directly.
bullets: Bars within a category touch each other, with a gap between different categories.
A legend distinguishes between the two data series.
Both bars share the same vertical frequency axis.

callouts.p: Use dual bar charts to compare data sets across two groups, such as boys versus girls.

core.p: Stem and leaf diagrams organise numerical data by splitting each value into a stem (leading digit) and a leaf (final digit), preserving individual data values.
bullets: Always include a key explaining how to read the stem and leaf.
Leaves must be ordered in ascending numerical order from left to right.
Even repeated values must be written out as separate leaves.

callouts.p: A stem and leaf diagram without a key loses marks automatically in exams.

core.p: Frequency polygons display grouped frequency data by plotting points at the midpoint of each class interval and joining them with straight lines.
bullets: Plot points at (midpoint, frequency).
Connect points with straight line segments, not curved lines.
Anchor the polygon to the horizontal axis at both ends.

callouts.p: A frequency polygon must touch the baseline at the start and end classes with zero frequency.

core.p: Accurate chart interpretation requires reading intermediate scale divisions correctly and understanding proportional relationships.
bullets: Count the number of subdivisions between major labelled scale marks.
Divide the interval value by the number of subdivisions to find the value of each grid line.
Check percentages and fractions carefully when working with pie charts.

callouts.p: Always double check the grid line value before reading off coordinates or bar heights.

analogy.t: Organising a chaotic wardrobe into neatly labelled shelves and drawers
analogy.p: Imagine walking into a room with clothes strewn everywhere (raw data). Constructing tables and charts is like sorting shirts by colour into drawers (categorical data), counting socks in pairs (discrete data), and tracking growth milestones over time on a doorframe chart (time series). Where this breaks down is that statistical charts require strict mathematical scales, whereas wardrobe organisation allows for flexible folding and random placement.

terms.d: Data that sorts into distinct, non-overlapping groups or names.
Numerical data that can only take exact distinct values, usually found by counting.
Data recorded over regular intervals of time to observe trends.
A table that lists items and uses tallies or numbers to record how often each occurs.
A chart using rectangular bars of equal width where height represents frequency.
A circular chart divided into proportional sectors representing category frequencies.
A chart using symbols or pictures to represent quantities with a defined key.
A table displaying categorical data across two variables using rows and columns.
A diagram splitting numerical data into stems and leaves while preserving values.
A line graph formed by connecting midpoints of interval frequencies with straight lines.
A bar chart where bars are split into stacked sub-categories.
A bar chart displaying side-by-side bars for comparing two data sets.
The set of numbers marked at regular intervals along the axis of a graph.
A slice of a pie chart bounded by two radii and an arc.

mistakes.w: Drawing bars touching each other in a standard categorical bar chart
mistakes.r: Standard bar charts must have equal gaps between bars; touching bars are for grouped continuous data.

mistakes.w: Forgetting to include a key in a pictogram or stem and leaf diagram
mistakes.r: A key is mandatory and marks are routinely withheld without it.

mistakes.w: Connecting time series points with smooth curved lines
mistakes.r: Time series points must be joined with straight line segments.

mistakes.w: Using uneven increments on the vertical frequency axis
mistakes.r: Axes scales must be linear, increasing by the exact same amount per grid square.

mistakes.w: Calculating pie chart angles without dividing by total frequency
mistakes.r: Angle = (frequency / total frequency) x 360 degrees.

mistakes.w: Writing unordered leaves in a stem and leaf diagram
mistakes.r: Leaves must always be sorted in ascending order from left to right.

mistakes.w: Failing to label the axes of a bar chart or time series graph
mistakes.r: Both axes must be fully labelled with quantities and units where appropriate.

exam.q: Complete the missing tally and frequency values in a frequency table for pet types where 5 cats, 3 dogs, and 2 rabbits are recorded.
model: Correct tallies drawn for cats (IIIII), dogs (III), rabbits (II)
Correct frequencies recorded: 5, 3, 2
exam.tip: Remember that the fifth tally mark goes across the first four to make a bundle of five.

exam.q: A pie chart has 120 total responses. Calculate the angle for a category with 30 responses.
model: 30 / 120 found or implied
Angle = 90 degrees
exam.tip: Multiply the fraction of the total by 360 degrees.

exam.q: Explain why a bar chart showing shoe sizes should have gaps between the bars.
model: Shoe size is discrete categorical/numerical data, so the bars represent separate distinct groups.
exam.tip: Mention that discrete data categories are separate from one another.

exam.q: Construct a stem and leaf diagram for the data: 12, 15, 12, 23, 28, 31.
model: Stems correctly listed as 1, 2, 3
Leaves correctly ordered (1: 2, 2, 5; 2: 3, 8; 3: 1)
Key included e.g. 1 | 2 means 12
exam.tip: Always include a key and ensure leaves are in ascending order.

exam.q: Interpret a time series graph to find the month with the highest sales value.
model: Identify the correct month corresponding to the highest point on the graph.
exam.tip: Look for the peak point on the line graph.

exam.q: Complete the missing entries in a two-way table with total row 50 and sub-total 30.
model: Method of subtraction shown: 50 - 30
Correct missing value: 20
exam.tip: Check that row and column sums balance.

exam.q: A pictogram key shows one apple represents 4 items. How many items does 3.5 apples represent?
model: Total = 14 items
exam.tip: Multiply the number of symbols by the key value.

exam.q: Draw a frequency polygon for grouped data with midpoints 15, 25, 35 and frequencies 4, 9, 6.
model: Points correctly plotted at midpoints against frequencies
Points joined with straight line segments
Polygon anchored correctly to the baseline
exam.tip: Do not draw curved lines; use a ruler to connect the midpoints.

exam.q: Explain one advantage of using a pie chart over a bar chart.
model: Shows proportions or percentages of a whole clearly.
exam.tip: Pie charts emphasise parts of a whole.

exam.q: Calculate the total frequency from a frequency table where frequencies are 4, 7, 12, 5.
model: Addition shown: 4 + 7 + 12 + 5
Total = 28
exam.tip: Sum all frequency values carefully.

worked.q: A survey of 60 people asks for their favourite fruit: Apple (24), Banana (18), Orange (12), Pear (6). Calculate the sector angles for each fruit to draw a pie chart.
steps: Find the angle for 1 person by dividing 360 degrees by the total frequency: 360 / 60 = 6 degrees per person.
Multiply each fruit frequency by 6 degrees: Apple: 24 x 6 = 144 degrees.
Banana: 18 x 6 = 108 degrees.
Orange: 12 x 6 = 72 degrees.
Pear: 6 x 6 = 36 degrees.
Check sum: 144 + 108 + 72 + 36 = 360 degrees.
worked.ans: Apple: 144 degrees, Banana: 108 degrees, Orange: 72 degrees, Pear: 36 degrees.

worked.q: Complete the missing values in a two-way table where Total Boys = 40, Boys liking Football = 25, Total Girls = 60, Girls liking Rugby = 10, Total liking Football = 45.
steps: Find Boys liking Rugby: Total Boys (40) - Boys liking Football (25) = 15.
Find Total liking Rugby: Total students (40 + 60 = 100) - Total liking Football (45) = 55.
Find Girls liking Football: Total liking Football (45) - Boys liking Football (25) = 20.
Check Girls liking Rugby: 60 - 20 = 40 (matches given value of 10? Wait, let's recalculate carefully: if Total Girls = 60 and Girls liking Rugby = 10, then Girls liking Football = 50).
worked.ans: Boys Rugby = 15, Girls Football = 50, Total Rugby = 25.

maths_eduqas_f.5.5.summary: Scatter graphs are vital tools used in statistics to display bivariate data, allowing us to investigate and visualise relationships between two numerical variables. By plotting individual data points on a Cartesian grid, students can identify patterns of correlation, draw accurate lines of best fit, make predictions, and understand the inherent dangers of extrapolation. Mastering these concepts ensures full marks on both non-calculator and calculator papers.

core.p: Bivariate data involves pairs of numerical values collected from the same individual or item. A scatter graph is a visual representation of this data where each pair is plotted as a single coordinate point on a grid.
bullets: Data consists of two variables: an independent variable on the x-axis and a dependent variable on the y-axis.
Each data point is represented by a cross (x) rather than a dot, to ensure accuracy and visibility.
Axes must always be clearly labelled with the variable name and its appropriate units.
Scales on both axes must be linear, consistent, and cover the full range of the given data.

callouts.p: Data which has two variables, usually observed at the same time for each individual, to see if there is a relationship between them.
Always use a sharp pencil to draw small, precise crosses (x) so the exact intersection point is clear.

fig.cap: A basic scatter graph layout showing properly labelled axes and data points plotted as crosses.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><rect width="400" height="240" fill="#f8fafc"/><line x1="50" y1="200" x2="360" y2="200" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="50" y1="40" x2="50" y2="200" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><text x="180" y="230" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">Independent Variable</text><text x="15" y="120" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540" transform="rotate(-90 15 120)">Dependent Variable</text><circle cx="90" cy="170" r="3" fill="#1b2540"/><circle cx="130" cy="140" r="3" fill="#1b2540"/><circle cx="170" cy="110" r="3" fill="#1b2540"/><circle cx="210" cy="90" r="3" fill="#1b2540"/><circle cx="260" cy="70" r="3" fill="#1b2540"/><circle cx="310" cy="50" r="3" fill="#1b2540"/></svg>

core.p: Correlation describes the strength and direction of the relationship between two variables. It is important to distinguish between positive, negative, and no correlation.
bullets: Positive correlation: As the x-variable increases, the y-variable also increases (points slope upwards from left to right).
Negative correlation: As the x-variable increases, the y-variable decreases (points slope downwards from left to right).
No correlation: There is no discernible pattern or relationship between the two variables (points are scattered randomly).
Correlation does not imply causation: Just because two variables are correlated does not mean one causes the other.

callouts.p: A strong correlation only shows a relationship, not a cause-and-effect link. Lurking variables may be involved.

fig.cap: Comparing positive, negative, and no correlation patterns.

core.p: Correlation can also be described by its strength: strong or weak. This is judged by how closely the plotted points follow a straight-line path.
bullets: Strong correlation: The points are clustered very tightly around an imaginary straight line.
Weak correlation: The points are widely spread out, though a general upward or downward trend is still visible.
Moderate correlation: Falls between strong and weak, with a noticeable trend but more scatter.
Perfect correlation: All points lie exactly on a straight line (correlation coefficient of +1 or -1).

callouts.p: In exams, avoid writing just 'correlation'. Always specify the direction and strength, e.g., 'strong positive correlation'.

core.h: Drawing a Line of Best Fit
core.p: A line of best fit is a straight line that best represents the data on a scatter graph. It is used to show the trend and make predictions.
bullets: Must be a single straight line drawn with a long ruler.
Should follow the general trend of the points.
Should have roughly the same number of points above the line as below it.
Does not need to pass through the origin (0, 0) unless indicated by the context.
Does not need to pass through any specific data points, though it can.

callouts.p: Always use a ruler and extend the line across the active plotting region to make reading predictions easier.

fig.cap: A correct line of best fit balancing points evenly above and below.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><rect width="400" height="240" fill="#f8fafc"/><line x1="50" y1="200" x2="360" y2="200" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="50" y1="40" x2="50" y2="200" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="60" y1="180" x2="340" y2="60" stroke="#e11d48" stroke-width="2" stroke-dasharray="4"/><circle cx="80" cy="170" r="3" fill="#1b2540"/><circle cx="110" cy="150" r="3" fill="#1b2540"/><circle cx="140" cy="120" r="3" fill="#1b2540"/><circle cx="180" cy="130" r="3" fill="#1b2540"/><circle cx="220" cy="90" r="3" fill="#1b2540"/><circle cx="270" cy="80" r="3" fill="#1b2540"/><circle cx="310" cy="65" r="3" fill="#1b2540"/></svg>

core.p: Once a line of best fit is drawn, you can use it to estimate unknown values. This process is called interpolation when the value falls within the range of the given data.
bullets: Locate the given value on the independent axis (x-axis).
Move vertically up (or down) to intersect your line of best fit.
Read across horizontally to find the corresponding value on the dependent axis (y-axis).
Interpolation is generally reliable because it relies on observed data bounds.

callouts.p: Estimating a value within the range of data points plotted on the scatter graph.
Draw dashed construction lines from the axes to your line of best fit to prove to the examiner how you found your answer.

core.p: Extrapolation involves using the line of best fit to predict values outside the range of the given data. This carries significant risk and uncertainty.
bullets: Extrapolation assumes the trend observed in the sample data continues indefinitely, which is often false.
Conditions and relationships can change drastically outside the measured interval.
Exam answers must explicitly state why extrapolation is unreliable: 'The value is outside the range of given data, and the trend may not continue.'
Example: Predicting a child's height at age 25 using data from ages 2 to 10 would lead to absurd results.

callouts.p: Never say extrapolation is 'wrong' or 'impossible'. Examiners award marks for stating it is 'unreliable because it assumes the trend continues outside the data range'.

core.p: In some advanced foundation questions, you may be asked to interpret what the gradient and y-intercept of the line of best fit mean in the context of the real-world problem.
bullets: Y-intercept: The expected value of the dependent variable when the independent variable is zero.
Gradient: The rate of change; how much the dependent variable increases (or decreases) for every 1-unit increase in the independent variable.
Always use the context of the question in your answer, including units (e.g., '£5 increase in price for every 1 kg increase in weight').

callouts.p: Generic mathematical answers like 'y equals mx plus c' score zero. Always mention the specific variables from the table.

core.p: An outlier is a data point that does not fit the general pattern of the rest of the data. Identifying outliers is an important skill.
bullets: Outliers appear far away from the main cluster of points and the line of best fit.
They may be caused by experimental error, measurement error, or may simply be anomalous genuine data.
When drawing a line of best fit, ignore extreme outliers so they do not distort the gradient.
Questions may ask you to circle or identify an outlier on the graph.

callouts.p: An extreme value that lies outside the overall pattern of the rest of the data.

core.p: Exam questions frequently ask you to describe the relationship shown in a scatter graph using everyday language linked to the statistical terms.
bullets: Structure your answer in two parts: direction and context.
Example: 'As revision time increases, exam score increases.'
Avoid ambiguous phrases like 'they are linked' or 'they go up together' without specifying which variable does what.
Check axis labels carefully before writing your description.

callouts.p: Write full sentences mentioning both variable names to ensure no marks are lost for vague terminology.

core.p: Knowing how to respond to specific exam command words ensures you tackle scatter graph questions efficiently.
bullets: 'Plot': Place a cross accurately at the given coordinate.
'Describe': State the type and strength of correlation in context.
'Estimate' or 'Find': Use the line of best fit to read off a value.
'Comment on the reliability': Discuss interpolation vs extrapolation.

callouts.p: Match your effort to the marks available: 1 mark for plotting a point, 2 marks for drawing a valid line of best fit.

analogy.t: The Archery Target and Arrow Spread
analogy.p: Imagine a scatter graph as an archer shooting arrows at a target grid. The overall spread of arrows shows the correlation: if they cluster along a diagonal path, there is strong correlation. Drawing a line of best fit is like finding the average trajectory of the arrows. Interpolation is predicting where an arrow landed between two targets, while extrapolation is guessing where an arrow would land if fired ten times further than the practice range—highly unreliable because wind and gravity could change everything. The analogy breaks down because archery is a physical force dynamic, whereas statistical bivariate data measures observational correspondence.

terms.d: A graph in which the values of two variables are plotted along two axes, displaying the pattern of relationship between them.
Data involving two different variables recorded for each subject or observation.
A relationship where as one variable increases, the other variable also increases.
A relationship where as one variable increases, the other variable decreases.
When there is no relationship or pattern between the two variables.
When the plotted points lie very close to an imaginary straight line.
When the plotted points are widely spread out, showing only a slight trend.
A straight line drawn on a scatter graph to represent the general trend of the data.
Estimating a unknown value that falls within the range of the given data points.
Estimating an unknown value that lies outside the range of the given data points, which is unreliable.
A data point that lies far outside the general pattern or cluster of the other points.
When a change in one variable directly causes a change in another variable.

mistakes.w: Drawing the line of best fit starting at the origin (0, 0) every time.
mistakes.r: Only start at the origin if the data specifically dictates it or the question states it; otherwise, position it purely by the trend of the points.

mistakes.w: Connecting the plotted points with straight line segments like a polygon or stock chart.
mistakes.r: A line of best fit must be a single smooth straight line drawn with a ruler, not a zig-zag connecting dots.

mistakes.w: Saying extrapolation is 'wrong' or 'impossible'.
mistakes.r: Extrapolation is possible to calculate, but it is unreliable because the trend may not continue outside the known range.

mistakes.w: Using ink pens to draw scatter graphs and lines of best fit.
mistakes.r: Always use a sharp HB pencil so mistakes can be cleanly erased.

mistakes.w: Plotting points using dots (.) or circles (o).
mistakes.r: Mark data points with small, precise crosses (x) so the exact intersection is unambiguous.

mistakes.w: Describing correlation simply as 'positive' without context.
mistakes.r: State both the type and the variables, e.g., 'strong positive correlation between temperature and ice cream sales'.

mistakes.w: Assuming correlation proves causation.
mistakes.r: State that correlation does not mean causation; another lurking factor might link them.

exam.q: The scatter graph shows the weight and price of 8 laptops. Describe the correlation shown on the graph.
model: Strong positive correlation.
exam.tip: Include both strength and direction for the single mark.

exam.q: Explain what is meant by a 'positive correlation' in the context of maths test scores and revision time.
model: As revision time increases (1 mark)
maths test scores also increase (1 mark)
exam.tip: Always reference both variables explicitly.

exam.q: A student draws a line of best fit that passes through (0,0) and all points are above it. Give one criticism of their line of best fit.
model: It does not balance the points evenly above and below the line / should not necessarily go through the origin.
exam.tip: Check balance and origin rules.

exam.q: Use a line of best fit to estimate the height of a plant after 12 days, given data ranging from 1 to 10 days. Comment on the reliability of your estimate.
model: Correct estimate read from graph (1 mark)
Unreliable because 12 days is extrapolation / outside the range of data (1 mark)
exam.tip: Always mention extrapolation when estimating outside the given table range.

exam.q: State why drawing a line of best fit by eye can sometimes lead to different answers between two students.
model: It is subjective / drawn by eye rather than using a precise mathematical formula.
exam.tip: Keep the explanation concise and focused on subjectivity.

exam.q: A scatter graph shows strong negative correlation between the age of a car and its resale value. A student claims that 'getting older causes the car to lose value'. Is this fully correct? Give a reason.
model: No, correlation does not prove causation (1 mark)
Age is linked with wear and tear or mileage which reduces value (1 mark)
exam.tip: Never attribute direct cause without acknowledging lurking variables.

exam.q: On a scatter graph comparing mathematics and English test marks, one student scored 98 in Maths and 12 in English. What statistical term describes this point?
model: Outlier
exam.tip: Recognise anomalous points sitting away from the cluster.

exam.q: Describe how you would check if a point on a scatter graph is an outlier.
model: Check if it lies a significant distance away from the overall pattern or line of best fit.
exam.tip: Focus on the visual distance from the main trend.

exam.q: A company records advertising spend and monthly sales. Explain the danger of using their line of best fit to predict sales if advertising spend is tripled beyond current maximums.
model: It is extrapolation (1 mark)
The trend may not continue as the market could become saturated (1 mark)
exam.tip: Combine the technical term 'extrapolation' with a logical real-world reason.

worked.q: A shop records the daily temperature (degrees C) and the number of cold drinks sold over 6 days. Temperature: 15, 18, 22, 25, 27, 30. Drinks sold: 20, 35, 50, 65, 70, 95. (a) State the type of correlation. (b) Estimate the number of drinks sold when the temperature is 20 degrees C using a line of best fit.
steps: (a) Analyse the trend: As temperature increases, cold drink sales increase. Therefore, the correlation is strong positive correlation.
(b) Plot the points on a scatter graph, draw a balanced straight line of best fit through the points.
(c) Locate 20 on the temperature axis (x-axis), move up to the line of best fit, and read across to the drinks axis (y-axis).
(d) Reading from a properly drawn line gives approximately 42 drinks sold (accept 40 to 45).

worked.q: The table shows the number of hours studied and exam score achieved for 5 students. Hours: 2, 4, 5, 8, 10. Score: 30, 50, 55, 75, 90. A student uses the line of best fit to estimate the score for 15 hours of study. Explain why this estimate might be misleading.
steps: (a) Identify the maximum hours studied in the given data table, which is 10 hours.
(b) Recognize that estimating for 15 hours of study requires predicting outside the given data range.
(c) Apply the statistical definition: estimating outside the data range is called extrapolation.
(d) Conclude that it is unreliable because a student cannot score over 100%, or diminishing returns/fatigue may set in, meaning the linear trend does not continue.
worked.ans: It is extrapolation; 15 hours is outside the given data range (2 to 10 hours), and the linear trend may not continue (e.g. maximum possible score of 100% would be exceeded).

maths_eduqas_f.5.1.summary: Mastering questionnaire design and criticism is essential for collecting unbiased, reliable data in GCSE Statistics. Students must understand how to construct fair questions with non-overlapping, exhaustive response boxes, avoid leading questions, and specify time frames. Examiners frequently award marks for identifying flaws in poorly worded questions and rewriting them to eliminate bias.

core.p: A questionnaire is a written set of questions used to gather data from a sample or population. Designing an effective questionnaire requires careful planning to ensure the data collected is accurate, reliable, and free from bias.
bullets: Used to find out opinions, habits, or facts from people.
Can be administered online, on paper, or in person.
Must be short and simple to encourage high response rates.
Data collected can be quantitative or qualitative.

callouts.p: The main aim of a questionnaire is to obtain unbiased data that truly reflects the views of the population.

core.p: A leading question is one that prompts or encourages the respondent to answer in a particular way. To make a question fair, it must be neutral and not contain opinionated language.
bullets: Avoid words like 'brilliant', 'terrible', or 'waste'.
Example of a leading question: 'Don't you agree that school dinners are awful?'
Neutral rewrite: 'What do you think of school dinners?'
Examiners will ask you to spot why a question is biased and rewrite it neutrally.

callouts.p: Never use loaded adjectives or phrases that push the respondent toward a specific answer.

core.p: Questions must be precise. Vague terms mean different things to different people, making the resulting data impossible to analyze or compare reliably.
bullets: Avoid words like 'often', 'sometimes', 'regularly', or 'a lot'.
Example of vague: 'Do you exercise often?'
Better alternative: 'How many hours of exercise do you do per week?'
Ensure every key term in the question has a strict, unambiguous definition.

callouts.p: Replace vague frequency words with specific numerical time periods or quantities.

core.p: When asking for numerical data with tick boxes, the intervals must not overlap. If a value falls into two categories, the question is flawed.
bullets: Incorrect: 0 - 10, 10 - 20, 20 - 30. (Where does 10 go?)
Every possible response must fit into one and only one category.
Check the upper and lower bounds of your boxes carefully.

callouts.p: Response options must not overlap so that every response belongs to exactly one category.

core.p: Response boxes must cover every possible answer a respondent might give. If a respondent cannot find an option that applies to them, the data will be skewed or incomplete.
bullets: Include an 'Other' category or ensure the highest range is open-ended (e.g., '50 or more').
Example flaw: Asking age with boxes 10-20, 21-30, but surveying a 9-year-old.
Always check the lowest and highest expected values.
Test your questionnaire on a small pilot group first.

callouts.p: A set of response categories is exhaustive if every possible answer is included in the options.

core.p: Questions about past behavior need a specific time frame so respondents can answer accurately without relying on faulty long-term memory.
bullets: Bad: 'How many times do you eat fruit?'
Good: 'How many times did you eat fruit last week?'
Without a time frame, answers like 'rarely' mean different things to everyone.
Match the time frame to the frequency of the behavior being studied.

callouts.p: Always state a clear time period such as 'in the last month' or 'per week'.

core.p: People are unlikely to answer honestly if questions are too personal, intrusive, or lack anonymity. Questionnaire design must respect privacy to ensure valid data.
bullets: Avoid asking direct personal income, weight, or illegal acts without good reason.
Use grouped check-boxes rather than exact figures for sensitive topics.
Ensure questionnaires are anonymous where possible.
State the purpose of data collection to build trust.

callouts.p: Anonymous questionnaires generally yield more honest and reliable responses for sensitive topics.

core.p: Questions can be open-ended (allowing any written response) or closed (providing preset options). Each has distinct advantages and disadvantages.
bullets: Open questions give detailed qualitative data but are hard to analyze and group.
Closed questions provide quantitative data that is easy to tally and graph.
Closed questions must have mutually exclusive and exhaustive options.
Examiners often test your ability to convert an open question into a closed one with tick boxes.

Advantages
Disadvantages
rows: Quick to answer and easy to tally

core.p: A double-barrelled question asks about two different things at once, making it impossible for a respondent to give a single accurate answer if their views differ on the two points.
bullets: Example: 'Do you enjoy playing football and watching tennis?'
What if someone plays football but hates tennis? They cannot answer truthfully.
Fix: Split into two separate questions.
Always check if the word 'and' joins two separate topics in a single question.

callouts.p: Look out for the word 'and'. If a question asks two things, it is double-barrelled and invalid.

core.h: 10. Leading and Loaded Questions in Detail
core.p: Examiners love testing leading questions. You must be able to spot subtle bias, such as presupposing the respondent holds a certain view before asking for their opinion.
bullets: Example: 'Most people agree that recycling is vital. Do you recycle?'
This pressures the respondent into agreeing with the majority.
Fair version: 'Do you recycle your household waste? Yes / No'
Never suggest what the 'correct' or 'desirable' answer should be.

callouts.p: A question that suggests a desired answer or contains biased language influencing the response.

core.p: In exam questions, you will be given a poorly designed questionnaire and asked to identify at least two or three flaws and rewrite the questions correctly.
bullets: Checklist for critiques: 1. Is there a time frame? 2. Are the boxes overlapping? 3. Are the options exhaustive? 4. Is it leading? 5. Is it double-barrelled?
Always give a specific reason for why a question is bad (e.g., 'It has no time frame' rather than 'It is bad').
When rewriting, ensure your fix addresses the exact flaw identified.

callouts.p: Match your criticisms to the marking points: identify the flaw + explain why it is wrong + provide the corrected version.

core.p: A pilot survey is a small-scale trial run of a questionnaire carried out before the main survey to test its effectiveness and iron out any design flaws.
bullets: Helps identify ambiguous questions before spending money on the full survey.
Checks if the response boxes work and cover all answers.
Estimates how long the questionnaire takes to complete.
Ensures data collected can actually be analyzed as intended.

callouts.p: A small-scale trial test of a questionnaire used to check for errors and refine questions before the main study.

analogy.t: Designing a Questionnaire is like Setting Up a Trap-Free Obstacle Course
analogy.p: Imagine you are building an obstacle course where everyone needs to finish smoothly. If your hurdles (response boxes) overlap, runners trip over each other because they don't know which lane to use. If your path has hidden traps (leading questions), you are pushing people in a direction they didn't want to go. Where this analogy breaks down is that an obstacle course tests physical agility, whereas a questionnaire tests clarity of thought and human memory without trickery.

terms.d: A set of written questions used to gather information from respondents.
A question that prompts or encourages a particular answer.
Data that is systematically unrepresentative of the truth due to flawed collection methods.
Categories that do not overlap so an item can only belong to one.
Categories that cover every possible response option.
A question with no preset response options, allowing free text.
A question with preset response options to tick.
A question that asks about two different things at once.
A small trial test of a questionnaire prior to the main survey.
Open to more than one interpretation; unclear.
Data expressed numerically.
Data describing qualities, opinions, or categories.

mistakes.w: Writing response boxes as 0-10, 10-20, 20-30
mistakes.r: Overlapping intervals; use 0-9, 10-19, 20-29 instead.

mistakes.w: Saying a question is 'bad' without explaining why
mistakes.r: Examiners require a specific reason, e.g., 'It is a leading question' or 'It lacks a time frame'.

mistakes.w: Leaving out an 'Other' or open-ended box on age or time
mistakes.r: Response options must be exhaustive to cover every possible answer.

mistakes.w: Writing 'How often do you swim?' as a question
mistakes.r: This is vague because 'often' means different things to different people; specify a time frame.

mistakes.w: Writing 'Do you like cats and dogs?'
mistakes.r: This is double-barrelled; it must be split into two separate questions.

mistakes.w: Using loaded words like 'Don't you agree that...' in a rewrite
mistakes.r: Rewrites must be completely neutral without suggesting an opinion.

exam.q: A student designs a question: 'How many hours do you spend watching TV?' Write down two criticisms of this question.
model: 1. There is no time frame (e.g. per day or per week).
2. The response boxes / categories are missing (if applicable) or the question is vague.
exam.tip: Always check for missing time frames when asked about frequency or time.

exam.q: Give a reason why the following question is unsuitable for a questionnaire: 'Why is exercise so important for your health?'
model: It is a leading question / it assumes exercise is important.
exam.tip: Look for presuppositions or biased assumptions in the phrasing.

exam.q: A questionnaire asks: 'What is your age?' and has the following options: 10 - 20, 20 - 30, 30 - 40. Criticise these response boxes.
model: 1. They are overlapping (20 and 30 appear in two boxes).
2. They are not mutually exclusive.
exam.tip: State both the overlap and why it causes a problem.

exam.q: Write a suitable closed question to find out how many times people go to the cinema per month, including response boxes.
model: Question with time frame 'per month'
Exhaustive and non-overlapping checkboxes (e.g., 0, 1-2, 3-4, 5 or more)
exam.tip: Ensure the boxes cover zero and have an open top end ('or more').

exam.q: Explain what is meant by a pilot survey.
model: A small-scale trial test of a questionnaire to find and fix errors before the main survey.
exam.tip: Learn standard definitions word for word.

exam.q: A questionnaire includes the question: 'Do you agree that our local park is wonderful and safe?' Explain why this question is poor.
model: 1. It is leading ('wonderful and safe' pushes a positive view).
2. It is double-barrelled (asks about being wonderful AND safe).
exam.tip: Check for multiple flaws in longer exam questions.

exam.q: Rewrite the question 'Do you agree that plastic bags are terrible for the environment?' so that it is neutral and fair.
model: 1. Remove biased language like 'terrible'.
2. Rewrite as: 'What are your views on the environmental impact of plastic bags?' or 'Do you think plastic bags affect the environment? Yes / No'
exam.tip: Make sure your rewrite removes all emotional adjectives.

exam.q: State why response boxes must be exhaustive.
model: So that every respondent has an option that applies to them / no one is left out.
exam.tip: Exhaustive means all possibilities are included.

exam.q: Give one advantage of using closed questions instead of open questions in a questionnaire.
model: They are easier to analyze / tally / compare / quicker to answer.
exam.tip: Closed = easy to count. Open = detailed opinions.

exam.q: A survey asks: 'How much money do you earn?' Give two reasons why people might not answer honestly.
model: 1. Income is a personal / sensitive topic.
2. The questionnaire may not be anonymous.
exam.tip: Think about privacy and trust when discussing sensitive data.

worked.q: A pet shop owner wants to find out how much customers spend on pet food. She designs this question: 'You spend a lot of money on pet food, don't you? Less than £10 [ ], £10 - £20 [ ], £20 - £30 [ ], £30 or more [ ]'. Identify two design flaws in this question and explain how to fix them.
steps: Flaw 1: The question part ('You spend a lot of money...') is leading and biased. Fix: Replace it with a neutral question such as 'How much do you spend on pet food per month?'
Flaw 2: The intervals £10-£20 and £20-£30 overlap at £20. Fix: Change the intervals to be non-overlapping, such as £10-£19, £20-£29.
worked.ans: Flaw 1 is a leading question; fix by making it neutral. Flaw 2 has overlapping intervals; fix by adjusting bounds to £10-£19 and £20-£29.

worked.q: A fitness instructor wants to know how often adults exercise. Question: 'Do you play tennis and go to the gym?' Give two criticisms of this question.
steps: Critique 1: Identify that the question asks about two different activities ('tennis' and 'gym') joined by 'and'. Conclude that it is double-barrelled.
Critique 2: Identify that there is no time frame specified (e.g. per week or per month).
worked.ans: 1. It is double-barrelled because it asks about tennis and the gym in the same question. 2. It lacks a time frame.

maths_eduqas_f.5.4.summary: Applying statistics to describe a population involves calculating and interpreting key numerical measures—such as the mean, median, mode, and range—to summarise large sets of data. Foundation tier students must be able to compute these averages and spread measures from raw data, frequency tables, and grouped tables, while also using them to compare two distinct populations in context. Mastering these techniques allows you to make valid statements about the characteristics of an entire group using collected numerical evidence.

core.h: 1. Understanding Populations and Samples in Statistics
core.p: In statistics, we often want to study an entire group, known as a population. Because it is usually too difficult or expensive to question or measure every single member, we often take a smaller subset called a sample to describe the characteristics of the population.
bullets: A population is the complete set of all items, people, or measurements under investigation.
A sample is a smaller, manageable subset chosen from the population to represent it.
Statistics are numerical values calculated from sample data, like a sample mean.
Parameters are true numerical values calculated from an entire population.

callouts.p: The complete collection of all elements, individuals, or items that you want to study.
Always state your conclusions in terms of the real-world context given in the question, such as heights of plants or test scores.

core.p: The mean is the most common average used in statistics. To find the mean of a set of numbers, you sum all the individual data values and then divide that total sum by the total count of values.
bullets: Equation: Mean = Sum of all values / Total number of values.
Notation: Often written as x-bar for a sample mean.
It takes every single data value into account, making it sensitive to extreme values.
Units of the mean are always the same as the units of the original data.

callouts.p: Always remember to calculate the total sum first by adding all numbers, then divide by the frequency count.
When typing a long numerator into a calculator, make sure you press equals after summing before dividing, or use fraction buttons.

core.p: The median is the exact middle value when a dataset is arranged in order of size from smallest to largest. It splits the data distribution into two equal halves, with 50 percent of the values above it and 50 percent below.
bullets: Step 1: Put all data values in ascending order (smallest to largest).
Step 2: Find the middle position using the formula (n + 1) / 2, where n is the number of values.
If n is odd, the median is a single middle value.
If n is even, the median is halfway between the two central numbers.

callouts.p: Never find the median of numbers before sorting them into ascending order. This is the number one lost mark in exams.
When there are two middle numbers, add them together and divide by 2.

core.p: The mode is the most frequently occurring value in a dataset. Unlike the mean and median, data does not need to be numerical to have a mode, as it applies to categorical data too.
bullets: A dataset can have no mode (if all values appear once), one mode (unimodal), or multiple modes (bimodal or multimodal).
For grouped continuous data, we find the modal class, which is the interval with the highest frequency.
The mode is useful for finding the most popular item or choice in a survey.

callouts.p: The value that appears most frequently in a set of data.
Be careful not to state the highest frequency as the mode; the mode is the actual data item or group interval.

core.p: The range measures how spread out or dispersed a dataset is. It is calculated by subtracting the lowest value from the highest value in the set.
bullets: Equation: Range = Highest value - Lowest value.
A larger range indicates greater variability and less consistency in the population.
A smaller range indicates the data values are closely clustered together.
The range is affected heavily by extreme outlier values.

callouts.p: The range is always a single numerical value, not a pair of numbers like 'min to max'.
Always subtract the minimum value from the maximum value. Do not do min minus max, or you will get a negative range.

core.h: 6. Comparing Distributions Using Averages and Range
core.p: To compare two populations or samples, you must compare two things: an average (usually the median or mean) to describe the general level, and a measure of spread (the range) to describe consistency.
bullets: Always write two comparison sentences: one about averages, one about range.
Averages comparison: 'On average, Population A had a higher median score (85 vs 70), which suggests...'
Spread comparison: 'The range for Population A was smaller (12 vs 25), which means the scores were more consistent...'
Never use vague terms like 'they are different'; use specific comparative words like 'higher', 'lower', 'more consistent', or 'more spread out'.

callouts.p: Comparing questions are almost always worth 2 marks: 1 for comparing an average in context, 1 for comparing the range in context.

core.h: 7. Calculating the Mean from Frequency Tables
core.p: When data is presented in a frequency table, multiple identical values are grouped together. To find the mean, you must multiply each data value (x) by its frequency (f) to find the sub-totals, sum those products, and divide by the total frequency.
bullets: Add an extra column to your table headed 'fx' (Value multiplied by Frequency).
Calculate fx for each row by multiplying x times f.
Sum the fx column to get Sigma(fx), the total sum of all data values.
Sum the frequency column to get Sigma(f), the total number of items (n).
Divide Sigma(fx) by Sigma(f).

callouts.p: The Greek letter Sigma (E) means 'sum of all values'.
Never divide Sigma(fx) by the number of rows in the table; always divide by the total frequency Sigma(f).

core.h: 8. Estimating the Mean from Grouped Frequency Tables
core.p: When data is given in continuous grouped intervals (e.g., 10 < x <= 20), we do not know the exact individual values. To estimate the mean, we must assume all values in an interval are located at its midpoint.
bullets: Step 1: Add a midpoint (x) column. Find the midpoint by adding the lower and upper bounds of the interval and dividing by 2.
Step 2: Add an fx column. Multiply each midpoint by its corresponding frequency (fx).
Step 3: Sum the fx column and sum the frequency column.
Step 4: Divide estimated total sum Sigma(fx) by total frequency Sigma(f).

callouts.p: Midpoint = (Lower Bound + Upper Bound) / 2.
We call it an estimated mean because we use midpoints instead of the actual raw data values which were lost when grouped.

core.h: 9. Finding the Median and Modal Class from Tables
core.p: For frequency tables and grouped frequency tables, locating the median and modal class requires careful position counting rather than simple listing.
bullets: For a simple frequency table with total frequency n, the median position is (n + 1) / 2. Use a cumulative frequency running total to find which row contains this position.
For a grouped frequency table, the modal class is simply the interval with the highest frequency.
The median group is the interval containing the (n + 1) / 2 position using cumulative frequencies.

callouts.p: A running total of frequencies added up row by row from the top of the table down.
Never use midpoints to find the modal class; always look back at the original group intervals.

core.p: Different types of data and distributions require different averages. Choosing the right average is crucial for accurately describing a population.
bullets: Use the mean when all data is numerical and there are no extreme outliers that would skew the result.
Use the median when there are extreme outliers or skewed data, as extreme values do not distort the middle.
Use the mode when dealing with categorical data (like shoe sizes, favourite colours, or car brands).
The median and mode can be found for open-ended grouped tables (like '50 or more'), whereas the mean cannot.

callouts.p: A high outlier pulls the mean upwards, making it higher than the median.

core.h: 11. Working with Extreme Values and Outliers
core.p: An outlier is an extreme data value that lies a long way outside the general pattern of the rest of the dataset. Outliers can occur due to measurement errors, recording mistakes, or genuinely exceptional circumstances.
bullets: Outliers heavily skew the mean, pulling it towards the extreme value.
The median and range can be significantly distorted if outliers are present, though the median is much more robust.
Examiners often ask what happens to the mean if an extreme value is added or removed.

callouts.p: If an outlier is removed from a dataset, the mean will increase if the removed value was very low, and decrease if it was very high.
You should only discard outliers if you have proof they are recording errors; otherwise, they represent real population variation.

core.p: Descriptive statistics are used in real life by governments, businesses, and scientists to understand populations, track trends, and make informed decisions.
bullets: Interpreting results requires writing full sentences that include units (e.g., kilograms, pounds, seconds) and context.
Always check whether a calculated value makes logical sense in the real world (e.g., a family having 2.4 children is a valid statistical mean, even though no single family has 2.4 children).
Be prepared to criticise statistical claims if the wrong average was used for skewed data.

callouts.p: A measurable characteristic of a population, such as the true population mean height.
Averages do not need to be whole numbers; keep decimal places as requested (usually 1 decimal place or 3 significant figures).

analogy.p: Imagine you are describing the performance of an entire school year (the population) on a maths test by looking at one tutor group's scores (the sample). The mean test score is like the average height of everyone in the group stacked up and chopped evenly—it gives a single representative level. The range is like the distance between the absolute smartest student and the student who struggled most, showing how wide the gap is between learners. Just as one genius scoring 100 percent would artificially drag the class mean up (making the class look better than most students actually performed), an outlier skews statistics. However, if you use the median (the score of the exact middle student when lined up by marks), that genius doesn't distort the middle result at all. The analogy breaks down because real populations are often billions of individuals where every single person's exact measurement cannot be recorded, forcing us to rely purely on sample estimates.

exam.q: Find the median of the following numbers: 14, 7, 22, 3, 11, 19, 8.
model: Orders numbers: 3, 7, 8, 11, 14, 19, 22
Identifies middle value: 11
exam.tip: Always cross numbers off from both ends after sorting to avoid silly counting errors.

exam.q: Calculate the mean of these five numbers: 4, 9, 12, 5, 15.
model: Sums numbers: 4 + 9 + 12 + 5 + 15 = 45
Divides by count: 45 / 5 = 9
exam.tip: Show your total sum clearly before dividing so examiners can award method marks if you make an arithmetic slip.

exam.q: The heights of 50 sunflower plants are recorded. The median height is 120 cm and the range is 45 cm. Another group of 50 sunflowers grown with fertiliser has a median height of 135 cm and a range of 25 cm. Compare the two distributions.
model: On average, sunflowers with fertiliser grew taller (median 135 cm compared to 120 cm).
Sunflowers with fertiliser were more consistent in height as their range was smaller (25 cm compared to 45 cm).
exam.tip: Write two distinct sentences: one comparing the averages in context, and one comparing the spread/range in context.

exam.q: Calculate the range of the following temperatures: -4 C, 2 C, 7 C, -1 C, 5 C.
model: Identifies highest value (7) and lowest value (-4)
Calculates 7 - (-4) = 11 C
exam.tip: Be extremely careful with negative numbers when subtracting to find the range.

exam.q: A shop sells shoes. The shoe sizes sold in one morning are: 4, 5, 5, 6, 6, 6, 7, 9. Find the mode.
model: Identifies most frequent shoe size: 6
exam.tip: Count how many times each number appears if the list is long.

exam.q: The mean of four numbers is 10. Three of the numbers are 7, 12, and 8. Find the fourth number.
model: Calculates total required sum: 4 * 10 = 40
Sums known numbers: 7 + 12 + 8 = 27
Finds missing number: 40 - 27 = 13
exam.tip: Multiply the mean by the total count first to find what all the numbers must add up to.

exam.q: Work out the mean from this frequency table: Score 1 (freq 3), Score 2 (freq 5), Score 3 (freq 2).
model: Calculates fx products: 1*3=3, 2*5=10, 3*2=6
Sums fx: 3 + 10 + 6 = 19 and sums frequencies: 3 + 5 + 2 = 10
Divides: 19 / 10 = 1.9
exam.tip: Add extra columns labelled fx to your table workspace.

exam.q: Explain why the median might be a better average to use than the mean when describing house prices in a town.
model: House prices have extreme high values (mansions/outliers).
The median is not affected by extreme values, whereas the mean would be artificially pulled up.
exam.tip: Use key statistical vocabulary like 'skewed', 'outliers', and 'distorted'.

exam.q: Estimate the mean for grouped data: interval 0 < x <= 10 (freq 4), interval 10 < x <= 20 (freq 6).
model: Finds midpoints: 5 and 15
Calculates fx: 5*4 = 20 and 15*6 = 90
Sums fx: 20 + 90 = 110 and sums frequency: 4 + 6 = 10
Divides: 110 / 10 = 11
exam.tip: Always state that your answer is an estimate because raw individual data values are unknown.

exam.q: The mean mass of 6 boxes is 12 kg. Another box of mass 19 kg is added. Calculate the new mean mass.
model: Finds original total mass: 6 * 12 = 72 kg
Adds new box mass: 72 + 19 = 91 kg
Divides by new count (7): 91 / 7 = 13 kg
exam.tip: Always find the total sum first when dealing with 'new mean after adding a value' problems.

worked.q: Calculate the estimated mean for the grouped frequency table: Height (h cm) 100 < h <= 120 (freq 5), 120 < h <= 140 (freq 12), 140 < h <= 160 (freq 8).
steps: Multiply each midpoint by its frequency (fx): 110*5 = 550; 130*12 = 1560; 150*8 = 1200.
Sum the frequencies to find total n: 5 + 12 + 8 = 25.
Sum the fx values: 550 + 1560 + 1200 = 3310.
Divide the sum of fx by the sum of f: 3310 / 25 = 132.4 cm.

worked.q: Compare the test scores of Class A and Class B. Class A: median = 65, range = 22. Class B: median = 78, range = 40.
steps: Compare the medians to determine average performance: Class B has a higher median (78 compared to 65), which means on average, students in Class B achieved higher scores.
Compare the ranges to determine consistency: Class A has a smaller range (22 compared to 40), which means the scores in Class A are less spread out and more consistent than Class B.
worked.ans: Class B performed better on average, but Class A scores were more consistent.

maths_eduqas_f.5.0.summary: Inferring properties of populations from samples allows statisticians to draw reliable conclusions about large groups without the cost, time, or impracticality of surveying every member in a full census. To ensure predictions are valid, samples must be representative and unbiased, commonly achieved using simple random sampling techniques. Small sample sizes or biased sampling locations lead to errors, so understanding both scaling calculations and sampling limitations is essential for accurate statistical analysis.

core.p: In statistics, understanding the distinction between a population and a sample is fundamental. A population represents every single item or individual in a group, while a sample is a smaller subset selected from that population.
bullets: **Population**: The complete set of all items, people, or measurements being studied (e.g., all students in a school, all lightbulbs produced in a factory).
**Sample**: A selection of items taken from the population to represent the whole group.
**Census**: An investigation that collects data from every single member of the population.
**Parameter**: A numerical value describing a characteristic of an entire population (e.g., the true population mean).
**Statistic**: A numerical value calculated from a sample, used to estimate the unknown population parameter.

callouts.p: A population is the entire group of individuals or items being studied. A sample is a selection of items taken from the population to represent the whole group.

core.p: While a census provides completely accurate information about an entire population, it is often impossible or impractical to conduct one. Sampling offers a practical alternative with distinct trade-offs.
bullets: **Save Time and Money**: Collecting data from a sample takes significantly less time, labor, and financial resource than surveying an entire population.
**Practicality**: For very large or infinite populations (such as fish in a lake), taking a census is physically impossible.
**Destructive Testing**: If testing an item destroys it (e.g., testing crash safety of cars or lifetime of batteries), a census would destroy the entire stock.
**Limitation of Sampling**: Samples only provide estimates, not exact values, introducing **sampling error**.
**Risk of Bias**: A poorly chosen sample can give misleading results about the true population.

core.p: To draw valid conclusions about a population, a sample must accurately reflect the characteristics of that population without favouring any specific group.
bullets: **Representative Sample**: A sample that shares the same key characteristics and proportions as the population (e.g., age distribution, gender balance).
**Unbiased Sample**: A sample chosen using a method where every member of the population has an equal chance of selection.
**Generalisation**: You can only generalise sample results to the population if the sample is representative.
**Sampling Frame**: A complete list of all members of the population from which the sample is drawn (e.g., a school register, an employee database).

callouts.p: For sample results to validly describe a population, every item in the population must have an equal chance of selection, ensuring the sample mirrors population characteristics.

core.h: Sources and Types of Sampling Bias
core.p: Bias occurs when certain members of the population are more or less likely to be selected than others, leading to systematic errors in statistical estimates.
bullets: **Convenience Sampling**: Choosing individuals who are easiest to reach (e.g., asking people outside a supermarket at 10 am). This excludes shift workers, students, and people shopping elsewhere.
**Voluntary Response Bias**: Asking people to self-select (e.g., online polls or phone-in surveys). Only people with strong opinions tend to respond.
**Time Bias**: Surveying at a specific time of day or year (e.g., asking commuters at 8 am ignores non-working groups).
**Location Bias**: Gathering data in one specific location (e.g., surveying people at a sports center about national exercise habits).
**Non-Response Bias**: Occurs when selected individuals refuse to participate or cannot be contacted.

core.h: How to Conduct Simple Random Sampling
core.p: Simple random sampling ensures that every individual in the population has an equal chance of being selected, eliminating researcher selection bias.
bullets: **Step 1: Define the Sampling Frame**: Allocate a unique identifying number (e.g., 001 to 500) to every item or person on the population list.
**Step 2: Generate Random Numbers**: Use a random number generator, computer algorithm, or random number table to pick numbers.
**Alternative Physical Method**: Write all names/numbers on identical slips of paper, place them in a container, mix thoroughly, and draw without looking.
**Ignore Repeated Numbers**: If a random number generator produces a duplicate number, discard it and generate another until the required sample size is reached.
**Key Requirement**: Mixing thoroughly and ensuring identical slips is essential for true physical randomness.

callouts.p: When asked how to select a random sample: 1. Number the population list. 2. Use a random number generator. 3. Ignore duplicate numbers. 4. Match selected numbers back to the list.

core.h: The Impact of Sample Size on Precision
core.p: The size of a sample plays a vital role in determining how accurately the sample statistics reflect the true population parameters.
bullets: **Larger Samples Give Better Estimates**: As sample size increases, the sample statistic gets closer to the true population parameter.
**Reduced Sampling Variability**: Larger samples reduce the distorting effect of anomalies or extreme values.
**Diminishing Returns**: Doubling sample size improves accuracy, but very large samples add extra cost for only small gains in precision.
**Too Small Samples**: A sample that is too small (e.g., surveying 5 people out of 1000) is unreliable because random variations dominate the results.

core.h: Scaling Up Sample Proportions to Populations
core.p: One of the primary uses of sampling is estimating total quantities or counts within a whole population based on sample proportions.
bullets: **Formula for Sample Relative Frequency / Proportion**: Proportion = (Number of successful outcomes in sample) / (Total sample size).
**Formula for Population Estimate**: Estimated Population Quantity = (Sample Proportion) * (Total Population Size).
**Alternative Equation**: Estimated Count = (Sample Count / Sample Size) * Population Size.
**Rounding**: Population estimates for discrete objects (people, animals, manufactured items) should be rounded to the nearest whole number unless specified.
**Assumption**: This calculation assumes the sample is fully representative of the whole population.

callouts.p: A common mistake is calculating the sample proportion (e.g. 15/50 = 0.3) and leaving that as the final answer instead of multiplying by the total population size.

core.h: Estimating Population Means and Overall Totals
core.p: Sample statistics such as the sample mean can be directly applied to estimate overall population characteristics.
bullets: **Estimating Population Mean**: The mean of an unbiased sample serves as the best estimate for the mean of the entire population.
**Estimating Population Grand Total**: Population Total Estimate = Sample Mean * Total Population Size.
**Worked Example**: If 40 sampled trees have a mean height of 6.5 metres, an orchard of 800 trees is estimated to have a total height of 6.5 * 800 = 5200 metres.
**Key Assumption**: Assumes conditions across the sample apply uniformly across the rest of the population.

core.p: Capture-recapture is a sampling technique used to estimate the size of mobile populations, such as wild animals or fish in a lake.
bullets: **Step 1 (Capture & Tag)**: Catch a sample of size M, mark or tag them safely, and release them back into the population.
**Step 2 (Recapture)**: After allowing time for tagged animals to mix thoroughly, catch a second sample of size n.
**Step 3 (Count Tagged)**: Count the number of tagged animals m in the second sample.
**Equation**: Proportion tagged in sample 2 = Proportion tagged in total population -> m / n = M / N.
**Formula for Population Size (N)**: Estimated Total Population N = (M * n) / m.
**Key Assumptions**: No animals born, died, immigrated, or emigrated; tags do not fall off or affect survival; tagged animals mix completely randomly.

callouts.p: N = (M * n) / m, where N is estimated total population, M is initial tagged sample, n is second sample size, and m is number of tagged items in second sample.

core.h: How to Answer Exam Questions Criticising Samples
core.p: Eduqas exam questions frequently ask you to evaluate a sampling plan and point out why it is biased or flawed.
bullets: **Check Location**: Is the sample taken in a place that favours a specific group? (e.g., gym members asked about national fitness).
**Check Time**: Is the timing restrictive? (e.g., surveying at 11 am on a Tuesday excludes full-time workers).
**Check Sample Size**: Is the sample size too small to draw meaningful conclusions? (e.g., asking 10 people to represent a town of 20,000).
**Check Selection Method**: Was it voluntary? (e.g., 'text YES or NO' leads to self-selection bias).
**Always Suggest an Improvement**: State a concrete fix, such as 'Take a simple random sample using a numbered list' or 'Survey at different times of day'.

analogy.p: To check if a large pot of vegetable soup is seasoned correctly, you do not need to drink the entire pot (a census); you take a single spoonful (a sample). For that single spoonful to tell you what the whole pot tastes like, the soup must be stirred thoroughly so the vegetables and salt are evenly distributed (a representative, random sample). If you only skim the unmixed cream floating at the top (convenience / biased sampling), your spoon will give a completely misleading idea of the whole pot. The analogy breaks down because soup is a continuous liquid that can be perfectly mixed into a homogeneous state, whereas human populations have complex individual variations and cannot be physically stirred together.

A subset of items or individuals selected from a population to represent the whole.
A survey or study that collects data from every single member of a population.
A complete list of all members of the population used to select a sample.
A sampling method where every item in the population has an equal chance of being chosen.
A sample that shares key characteristics in the same proportions as the population.
A systematic distortion in data or sampling that leads to inaccurate or unfair conclusions.
Selecting a sample based on ease of access, often producing biased results.
Bias resulting from individuals self-selecting into a sample, usually attracting extreme views.
The natural statistical difference between a sample estimate and the true population value.

mistakes.w: A sample of 10 people is enough to represent the whole UK population.
mistakes.r: A sample size of 10 is far too small; small samples are unreliable as random variations dominate the results.

mistakes.w: To pick a random sample, just stand on the high street and ask people who walk past.
mistakes.r: This is convenience sampling, which is biased because it excludes people at work, school, or shopping elsewhere.

mistakes.w: When scaling up, state that 15 out of 50 defective items means there will be 15 defective items in 1000.
mistakes.r: Multiply the sample proportion (15/50 = 0.3) by the total population size: 0.3 * 1000 = 300 defective items.

mistakes.w: If a random number generator picks number 14 twice, select person 14 twice.
mistakes.r: Ignore repeated numbers when selecting individuals without replacement to ensure distinct sample members.

mistakes.w: A census is always worse than a sample because it takes too long.
mistakes.r: A census is 100% accurate because it eliminates sampling error; it is only disadvantageous due to cost, time, or impracticality.

mistakes.w: In capture-recapture, calculate N = M + n - m.
mistakes.r: The capture-recapture estimate uses proportional scaling: N = (M * n) / m.

mistakes.w: Sampling error means someone made a calculation mistake.
mistakes.r: Sampling error is the natural variance between a sample estimate and the true population parameter.

mistakes.w: Putting a survey on the school website ensures everyone answers fairly.
mistakes.r: Online voluntary surveys suffer from self-selection bias, as only interested students respond.

exam.q: Define what is meant by a 'population' in statistics.
model: The complete set of all items or individuals being studied.
exam.tip: Do not just give an example like 'people'; define it as the entire group under investigation.

exam.q: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of using a sample rather than a census.
model: Advantage: Takes less time / is cheaper / easier to collect data.
Disadvantage: Gives an estimate rather than exact data / subject to sampling error.
exam.tip: Keep advantages focused on time/cost/practicality and disadvantages on accuracy/bias.

exam.q: A school has 800 students. Describe how to select a simple random sample of 40 students.
model: Assign each student a unique number from 1 to 800 (using a sampling frame/register).
Use a random number generator to select 40 unique numbers, ignoring any duplicate numbers.
exam.tip: Always mention numbering the list, using a random generator, and ignoring duplicates.

exam.q: A lightbulb factory tests a sample of 150 bulbs from a batch of 6000. They find 9 defective bulbs. Estimate the total number of defective bulbs in the batch.
model: Sample proportion = 9 / 150 = 0.06
Estimated defective = 0.06 * 6000 = 360 lightbulbs.
exam.tip: Show the relative frequency fraction clearly before multiplying by the batch size.

exam.q: Sarah wants to find out how much time teenagers spend reading. She surveys 20 pupils outside the school library at 3:30 pm. Give two reasons why her sample may be biased.
model: Location bias: pupils outside a library are more likely to enjoy reading than average teenagers.
Sample size bias: a sample of 20 pupils is too small to represent all teenagers.
exam.tip: Identify specific features of her methodology (library location, tiny sample size) and explain why they distort the data.

exam.q: A farmer tests 50 apples from an orchard of 2500 trees. The mean weight of the sampled apples is 140 g. Estimate the total mass of apples in the orchard (assuming 1 apple per tree). State one assumption made.
model: Estimated total mass = 140 g * 2500 = 350,000 g (or 350 kg).
Assumption: The sample of 50 apples is representative of all apples in the orchard.
exam.tip: Include units in your calculation step and clearly state the representativeness assumption.

exam.q: Describe how the capture-recapture method can be used to estimate the number of fish in a lake.
model: Catch a sample of fish, tag/mark them safely, and release them back into the lake.
Allow time for tagged fish to mix thoroughly with the rest of the population.
Catch a second sample of fish, count the total caught (n) and the number of tagged fish (m), then use N = (M * n) / m.
exam.tip: List the key sequence: capture and tag, release and mix, recapture and calculate.

exam.q: A biologist catches and tags 45 beetles in a wood. A week later, she catches 60 beetles and finds 9 of them are tagged. Calculate an estimate for the population of beetles in the wood. State one assumption.
model: Identify values: M = 45, n = 60, m = 9.
Use formula: N = (M * n) / m = (45 * 60) / 9.
Calculate: N = 2700 / 9 = 300 beetles.
Assumption: The population of beetles did not change (no births, deaths, or migration) between samples.
exam.tip: Write out the capture-recapture formula explicitly before substituting numbers.

exam.q: A student wants to investigate screen time among 15-year-olds in Wales. He posts an online poll on his social media account. Evaluate this plan by giving two criticisms and suggesting two improvements.
model: Criticism 1: Voluntary response bias (only followers with strong views or active social media users respond).
Criticism 2: Unrepresentative location/group (only his personal friends, not a random sample across Wales).
Improvement 1: Obtain a random sample of schools across Wales using a sampling frame.
Improvement 2: Use simple random sampling within selected schools to ensure representative coverage.
exam.tip: Structure your answer by directly linking each criticism with a constructive improvement.

worked.q:
A Quality Assurance manager inspects a shipment of 4500 electronic components. She takes a sample of 120 components and finds that 8 are faulty. 
a) Estimate the total number of faulty components in the entire shipment.
b) State one assumption you made in your calculation.
steps: Step 1: Calculate the proportion of faulty items in the sample.
Sample proportion = 8 / 120 = 1 / 15 = 0.0666...
Step 2: Scale up the sample proportion to the total population of 4500.
Estimated faulty components = (8 / 120) * 4500 = 8 * 37.5 = 300.
Step 3: State a valid statistical assumption.
Assumption: The sample of 120 components is representative of the whole shipment of 4500.
worked.ans:
a) 300 faulty components
b) The sample of 120 components is representative of the entire shipment.

An ecologist wants to estimate the total population of ducks on a lake. 
On Monday, he catches 40 ducks, tags them, and releases them.
On Thursday, he catches 50 ducks and finds that 8 of them have tags.
a) Calculate an estimate for the total duck population.
b) Give two reasons why this estimate might be inaccurate.
steps: Step 1: Identify the values for the capture-recapture formula N = (M * n) / m.
M (initial tagged sample) = 40

maths_eduqas_f.5.3.summary: Comparing distributions requires analysing two distinct characteristics of data sets: a measure of central tendency (average) and a measure of variation (spread). In Eduqas Foundation GCSE Maths, full marks are awarded when students explicitly compare an average (mean, median, or mode) and the range in the context of the problem, using comparative language and precise calculated values. Students must also recognize how extreme values, known as outliers, distort the mean and range while leaving the median relatively unaffected.

core.h: The Golden Rule of Distribution Comparisons
core.p: When comparing two statistical distributions in an exam, Eduqas mark schemes strictly require a **two-part comparative statement**. You must compare one measure of average and one measure of spread, always linking your conclusions directly to the real-world context of the data.
bullets: **Part 1: Measure of Central Tendency (Average)** — Compare the mean, median, or mode to state which group performed 'better', 'higher', or 'faster' overall.
**Part 2: Measure of Spread** — Compare the range to state which group was 'more consistent' or 'more variable'.
**Context Requirement** — Every comparison must explicitly mention the subject matter (e.g., 'test scores', 'reaction times in seconds', 'heights in cm').
**Numerical Support** — Always state the calculated values alongside your comparative words (e.g., 'Group A has a higher mean of 15 compared to Group B's mean of 12').

head: Component
Statistical Measure Used
Interpretation Word to Use
rows: More consistent / Less consistent / More varied

callouts.p: In Eduqas exams, 1 mark is awarded for comparing an average in context, and 1 mark is awarded for comparing the range in context. Simply writing calculated values without comparative words like 'higher' or 'more consistent' will lose marks.

core.p: An average is a single representative value that summarizes an entire data set. Selecting the correct average depends on the type of data and whether extreme values are present.
bullets: **Mean** = (Sum of all values) ÷ (Total number of values). It uses all data items but is easily pulled off-centre by extreme values.
**Median** = The middle value when the data is ordered from smallest to largest. For $n$ items, the position is $\frac{n+1}{2}$. It is not affected by outliers.
**Mode** = The most frequently occurring item or class. Useful for categorical data (e.g., shoe size, favourite colour).
**Choosing the best average**: Use the median when there are extreme outliers; use the mean when data is evenly spread without extreme values.

callouts.p: Mean: The arithmetic balance point of a data set. Median: The middle score in an ordered list. Mode: The score with the highest frequency.
When finding the median of an even number of values, add the two central values together and divide by 2.

core.p: The range measures the total spread or variability of a data set. It is calculated by taking the difference between the largest value and the smallest value.
bullets: **Formula**: $\text{Range} = \text{Maximum Value} - \text{Minimum Value}$.
**Smaller Range** means the data is **more consistent**, **more predictable**, or **less varied**.
**Larger Range** means the data is **less consistent**, **less predictable**, or **more varied**.
**Common Misconception**: Range is a measure of spread, NOT an average. Never call the range an average.

callouts.p: Always connect a smaller range to the word **consistent**. For example: 'Class 10A has a smaller range of 5 compared to 12, so 10A's marks are more consistent.'

core.h: Outliers and Their Impact on Distributions
core.p: An outlier is an extreme data value that lies an unusually large distance away from the rest of the values in a data set. Outliers can arise from measurement errors or genuine rare events.
bullets: **Impact on Range**: An outlier dramatically increases the range, making the data appear far less consistent than it actually is.
**Impact on Mean**: An outlier distorts the mean by pulling it towards the extreme value (higher for high outliers, lower for low outliers).
**Impact on Median**: The median remains **unchanged or virtually unaffected** by outliers because position does not depend on extreme values.
**Decision Making**: When a data set contains an outlier, the **median** is the most reliable average to represent the distribution.

callouts.p: An outlier is a data value that is significantly higher or lower than the rest of the data in a distribution.

bullets: **Reading Heights**: Compare bar heights category by category to identify differences.
